why_angle: The cited Plugable pages and the StarTech, ACT and Club 3D datasheets list 240W and 40Gbps as two separate ratings. None of them says that a cable only gets 240 W if its e-marker reports 50 V/5 A EPR to the charger. None says the two ratings split past 1 m either, as Plugable's own 2 m active 40Gbps cable shows by stopping at 100 W, even though a 2 m cable was recommended to this shopper. This page states that mechanism, shows a measured e-marker readout and adds the length split. It also picks the same-price Thunderbolt 5 cable, which the rivals never show. Our UGREEN Thunderbolt 5 cable is left out of the table: every UGREEN page returned HTTP 429, so its length and certification could not be sourced. It is mentioned in the text at its sourced $45.99 and does not win a segment against Plugable's $34.95 cable.

page.title: Which USB-C cable does 240W charging and 40Gbps data at the same time (2026)? The ones that are e-marked for both
page.h1: USB-C cables that do 240W charging and 40Gbps data at the same time (2026)
page.desc: A USB-C cable does 240 W and 40 Gbps together only when its e-marker reports 50 V/5 A EPR and USB4 or Thunderbolt speed. Seven 0.8 m to 2 m cables compared at maker prices, November 2026.
page.answer: Short answer. A USB-C cable does 240W charging and 40Gbps data at the same time only if its e-marker reports 50 V/5 A EPR plus USB4 or Thunderbolt speed. Plugable's 1 m Thunderbolt 5 cable (TBT5-240W1M) does; Plugable's own 2 m active 40Gbps cable stops at 100 W.

cells.both: Yes; backward compatible with Thunderbolt 4, 3 and USB4 (Plugable)
Yes; USB-IF certified, out of stock at Plugable on 2026-11-17
No: 40 Gbps but capped at 100 W

page.after:
What the differences mean

  • Same price, twice the bandwidth: Plugable's TBT5-240W1M and TBT4-240W-1M both cost $34.95 and are both rated 240 W. 80 Gbps ÷ 40 Gbps = 2× the data rate for $0 more.
  • Cost per metre: TBT5-240W1M $34.95 ÷ 1 m = $34.95/m; TBT5-240W80R $38.95 ÷ 0.8 m = $48.69/m; Anker A84N1 $45.99 ÷ 1 m = $45.99/m; Belkin INZ005 $53.99 ÷ 1 m = $53.99/m.
  • What the extra metre costs in power: the 2 m TBT4-40G2M is rated 100 W, while the 1 m TBT4-240W-1M is rated 240 W. 240 − 100 = 140 W less, at $69.95 ÷ 2 m = $34.98/m.
  • Where 240 W comes from: 48 V × 5 A = 240 W. The USB Type-C spec requires an EPR cable to work at 53.65 V or more, which leaves room above 48 V.
  • Other Thunderbolt 5 cables: UGREEN's Thunderbolt 5 cable is also rated 80 Gbps and 240 W. It costs $45.99 at UGREEN's US store, $45.99 − $34.95 = $11.04 more than the Plugable {buy:ugreen-thunderbolt-5-cable-80gbps-240w}.
Your setupCable that fits
Laptop to a dock or SSD on the same desk, 1 m is enoughPlugable TBT5-240W1M
Ports on the back or side, the cable has to turn tightlyPlugable TBT5-240W80R (0.8 m, right-angle)
Only 40 Gbps devices, lowest pricePlugable USB4-240W-1M when back in stock, otherwise TBT4-240W-1M
Mac setup and you want Apple's cableApple Thunderbolt 5 Pro Cable, 1 m (240 W), not the Thunderbolt 4 Pro Cable (100 W)
The device is 2 m awayAn active cable whose maker states 240 W/EPR. Plugable's 2 m TBT4-40G2M is rated 100 W.

How a cable tells the charger it can carry 240 W and 40 Gbps at once

Before a USB PD 3.1 charger raises the voltage above 20 V, it asks the cable to identify itself. Granite River Labs, a USB test lab, sets out the rule: the cable's e-marker chip "must be set to EPR Mode Capable and provide notification that it supports 50V and 5A." The USB Type-C spec, as quoted by CNX Software, says every EPR cable shall be electronically marked as 50 V and 5 A capable. The same chip also reports the cable's data speed, so a cable that does both carries both ratings in one ID. ChargerLAB's POWER-Z tester read LG's 240 W USB4 cable as 50 V 5 A EPR and USB4 Gen3 40 Gb. ChargerLAB measured 0.79 V of voltage drop on that cable at 28 V 5 A.

Length is where the two ratings split. Plugable says a passive Thunderbolt 4 cable is typically 1 m at most, and many are 0.8 m. Passive Thunderbolt 5 cables reach 1 m, and 2 m needs active retimer chips. Plugable's own active 2 m Thunderbolt 4 cable is rated 100 W. Apple's Thunderbolt 4 Pro Cable runs Thunderbolt 4 and USB4 at up to 40 Gbps but "delivers a maximum of 100W". Apple's 1 m Thunderbolt 5 Pro Cable delivers up to 240 W. So for any cable over 1 m, a 40 Gbps rating is not enough: the maker has to state 240 W or EPR.

On the packaging, Granite River Labs notes that a USB-IF certified 40 Gbps cable must also list its wattage, and that wattage can only be 60 W or 240 W. The mark you want reads 40Gbps and 240W. A 60 W mark means the e-marker will not report EPR, and the charger will not go above 20 V.

Not recommended

Plugable TBT4-40G2M (2 m, active): at $69.95 it costs twice as much as the 1 m 240 W cables and is rated 100 W, so it fails the 240 W half of the job. Apple Thunderbolt 4 Pro Cable: it carries 40 Gbps, but Apple caps it at 100 W. Both carry a Thunderbolt logo, which is why they catch shoppers out.
